title: Rethinking Git for the Age of Coding Agents with GitHub Cofounder Scott Chacon

reader_summary.headline: GitHub Cofounder Scott Chacon explains how to update Git for AI coding agents.
reader_summary.overview: Scott Chacon argues that Git needs changes because AI agents struggle with its old commands. He suggests new tools can bridge the gap between human needs and machine efficiency. The goal is to create a system where agents can work together smoothly without breaking existing workflows.

key_points.text: Git was built for Linux commands, not for user-friendly tools or AI agents.
key_points.evidence_quote: The most widely used developer tool in the world was never designed. Gets started as plumbing commands for the Linux kernel team.

key_points.text: New tools like Git Botter allow agents and humans to use Git together without breaking compatibility.
key_points.evidence_quote: with getbother, you can go back and forth between get and getbother. Like we don't want to, it's not jiu-jitsu where you have to have some collocated thing that's a really different way of doing stuff.

key_points.text: The biggest challenge now is agreeing on what to build, not just writing the code.
key_points.evidence_quote: the constraint moves not to, can I produce the code, but can we agree on what we want, right?

notes: Matt Bornstein speaks with Scott Chacon, cofounder of GitHub and CEO of GitButler, about why Git's user interface has barely changed since 2005, how GitButler is rethinking version control for both humans and AI agents, and what the "next GitHub" might actually look like. They cover parallel branches, agent-optimized CLI design, the future of code review, and why the best engineers of the future will be the best writers. thesis: Scott Chacon argues that Git, originally designed as Unix plumbing for the Linux kernel, lacks a unified design philosophy and has evolved into a 'Frankenstein' tool that struggles with modern coding agents. He suggests that while the core data storage and transmission protocols should remain unchanged, the user interface requires a complete rethink to accommodate the new ergonomics of AI-assisted coding.
